projects.name: Olist MLOps
projects.problem: Predict whether an Olist e-commerce order will arrive late, and serve that prediction through a tested, monitored API instead of a notebook.
built: A FastAPI inference service around the fitted scikit-learn model, with schema and semantic input checks.
Feature engineering shared by the training notebooks and the service, with a parity check between them.
Prometheus metrics, two alert rules and an offline score-drift check.
DVC pointers for data and model files, an MLflow registry entry, and a GitHub Actions pipeline.
works: CI runs lint, formatting, 172 tests and a Docker build on every push.
A Kaggle notebook re-runs the pipeline from the raw Olist data and reproduces the saved test results.
The service never refits the model; it loads the saved preprocessor and classifier.
projects.architecture: Six notebooks prepare data and train; a FastAPI service loads the saved preprocessor and model; Docker Compose runs the API with Prometheus.
projects.stack: Python, scikit-learn, FastAPI, Docker, Prometheus, DVC, MLflow, GitHub Actions

evidence.text: GitHub Actions run 42863988828: 172 passed, lint and format clean; reproduced from a fresh clone on 2026-11-14.
Kaggle re-run from the raw CSVs on 2026-11-14: test PR-AUC 0.0670 and ROC-AUC 0.6115, matching the saved model.
Feature parity on 14,470 validation rows and 821 features, maximum difference 0, measured on the original workstation.
Purchase-time availability of every feature is not verified, and there is no DVC remote.

projects.status: Educational project, not deployed. The model is weak: test ROC-AUC 0.61 at a 4.28% late rate.
projects.role: My project in an MLOps training course. The model-evaluation write-up and the Kaggle reproduction were added in November 2026 with an AI coding agent.

trace.name: Olist orders
trace.note: Public Olist orders, items, payments and reviews, joined into one row per order.

trace.name: Chronological split
trace.note: Train, validation and test periods are split by purchase date, so the test period is later than anything used for fitting.

trace.name: Shared features
trace.note: Deterministic feature code used by both the notebooks and the service; explicit future and target fields are blocked.

trace.name: Model and threshold
trace.note: Logistic regression chosen on validation PR-AUC; the decision threshold is chosen on validation only.

trace.name: Feature parity
trace.note: A script compares the service's features with the saved training matrix before a release.

trace.name: Inference API
trace.note: FastAPI single and batch prediction endpoints with input checks and a model fingerprint in every response.

trace.name: Monitoring
trace.note: Prometheus metrics and alert rules; the drift check reports insufficient data below 200 scores instead of claiming no drift.

decisions: Reported the weak test result (ROC-AUC 0.61, accuracy below an always-on-time baseline at the chosen threshold) instead of accuracy alone.
Chose the threshold on validation only and used the later test period once.
Documented the point-in-time leakage risk of historical aggregates instead of claiming real-time readiness.
Kept data and model files out of Git, tracked by DVC pointers, and stated that a fresh clone cannot serve predictions.
tested: 172 tests in GitHub Actions (run 42863988828), reproduced from a fresh clone on 2026-11-14.
Kaggle re-run from raw data: test PR-AUC 0.06704 and ROC-AUC 0.6115, matching the saved bundle.
Validation ROC-AUC 0.746 and PR-AUC 0.125; test ROC-AUC 0.611 and PR-AUC 0.067 at a 4.28% late rate.
limits: Not verified for purchase-time inference: some aggregates may include later updates.
No DVC remote or published model, so a fresh clone runs the tests but cannot serve predictions.
No alert notification channel and no store joining predictions with outcomes.
The model's predictive value is weak; the project's value is the inference engineering.

projects.name: RAG Quality Lab
projects.problem: When a team changes a RAG system, it is hard to tell whether answers improved, or why one answer cited the wrong source.
built: An evaluation and debugging layer added to Onyx Community Edition, an open-source RAG platform.
Versioned test datasets, background runs and saved results for each test case.
Six retrieval and citation metrics, plus an optional LLM judge that cannot change them.
An admin dashboard, a read-only retrieval debugger, and rule-based checks for risky text in ingested documents.
works: Metrics leave a value undefined when it cannot be measured, instead of counting it as zero.
A failed test case is saved and the run continues.
If the judge fails, the case still succeeds with an empty judge score.
projects.architecture: Python and FastAPI services inside Onyx, Celery for background runs, SQLAlchemy migrations, and React admin pages.
projects.stack: Python, FastAPI, Celery, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic, TypeScript, React

evidence.text: All 411 unit tests I added passed on 2026-11-07: 236 backend and 175 frontend, with the database, LLM and task broker replaced by fakes.
Migrations, API routes and dashboard pages are in the code. The pages have not been viewed running.
Not run end to end, and not evaluated on a real document collection.

projects.role: My personal project: I added this layer to Onyx Community Edition. Onyx provides the platform, including its chat pipeline and connectors. The private repository is a derivative of it, and credits it in UPSTREAM.md. Its top-level README still needs to say so before any public release.

trace.name: Dataset version
trace.note: Test cases are frozen into an immutable dataset version, so two runs can be compared on exactly the same questions.

trace.name: Background run
trace.note: A Celery task works through the cases. A case that raises is saved as failed and the run continues, so one bad case cannot erase the others.

trace.name: Chat pipeline
trace.note: Each case calls the platform's existing evaluation entry point, which runs its chat pipeline inside a rolled-back transaction. So far this path has only been tested with a fake executor.

trace.name: Deterministic metrics
trace.note: Recall@k, precision@k, MRR, citation validity, citation density and cited context ratio. These are pure functions with no model calls, so equal inputs give equal scores.

trace.name: Optional LLM judge
trace.note: Scores correctness, groundedness and semantic citation coverage after the deterministic metrics are computed. If the judge is off or fails, the case stays successful with an empty score.

trace.name: Aggregate
trace.note: A metric that cannot be measured stays undefined and is skipped. It is never counted as zero, and the dashboard code shows it as a dash, so missing data cannot pass as a bad result.

trace.name: Review
trace.note: An admin dashboard shows run summaries and per-case results. A separate read-only debugger shows the ranked documents, scores and citations behind a past answer.

decisions: Separated what is measured from what is judged. An LLM judge cannot change a deterministic score.
Treated "not measurable" as different from zero across the metrics, API and interface.
Called the platform's existing chat pipeline for evaluation instead of writing a test-only copy.
Kept the prompt-injection and credential detectors narrow, to limit false alarms.
tested: Evaluation: 122 passed. Metrics 48, aggregation 17, judge 26, runner 27, dispatch 4.
Knowledge operations and ingestion security: 70 passed.
Retrieval debugger: 37 passed. Citation privacy: 7 passed.
Frontend: 175 passed in 17 suites, 106 of them for the evaluation dashboard and debugger.
Run at commit c28ad87 from a clean copy with the project's own environment. The database, LLM and Celery broker were replaced by fakes.
limits: Never run end to end against the full platform in this check, so the real chat path is untested.
No evaluation report on a real document collection yet.
This is an extension of Onyx, not an independent RAG platform.
The dashboard has not been viewed running.

projects.name: ClientPilot AI
projects.problem: One operator supporting several businesses on Facebook Messenger needs AI replies grounded in each client's own knowledge, without exposing one client's data or tokens to another.
built: Extended open-source DocsFlow (MIT license) into a single-operator support product with client records and per-client knowledge.
A background worker for Messenger: signature check, event claim, autopilot check and confidence check.
A LangGraph agent flow with a step limit, a tenant-scoped database wrapper and encrypted token storage.
works: The database wrapper adds the tenant filter and rejects a missing tenant, tested against a mock database.
A source scan fails if a Meta token could reach a URL or browser storage.
The search function takes only a query. Tenant and client IDs stay in server code.
projects.architecture: Next.js API routes, a QStash-signed worker, a LangGraph supervisor, Pinecone namespaces per client, and Supabase.
projects.stack: TypeScript, Next.js, LangGraph, Pinecone, Supabase, QStash, Meta Graph API

evidence.text: 41 of 41 security tests passed: 22 tenant-isolation tests against a mock, and a 19-check source scan.
Whole suite: 56 passed, 9 failed, 1 suite did not load. All three failing files are upstream DocsFlow tests I did not change. They are not fixed.
The worker and agent graph have no automated tests.
No live run against Meta, Pinecone or QStash is verified.

projects.role: I extended open-source DocsFlow by Nic Chin (MIT license). DocsFlow provides the base application. The agent graph, tenant wrapper, token vault, message worker and security tests are from my commits.

trace.name: Signed queue
trace.note: The worker accepts only requests with a valid QStash signature. Temporary failures return an error so the queue retries the message.

trace.name: Idempotency claim
trace.note: Each provider event is claimed through a unique index, so a retried delivery that has already finished is skipped.

trace.name: Tenant scope
trace.note: The Page ID resolves to a tenant and client. Client data is then read through a tenant-scoped wrapper that fails if the tenant is missing. Event and message logs use the service client with an explicit tenant ID.

trace.name: Autopilot check
trace.note: The client must be active with autopilot on. Otherwise the message is logged as skipped and nothing is sent.

trace.name: Supervisor graph
trace.note: A LangGraph supervisor routes between research, synthesis, drafting and abstention. A budget of 5 steps forces abstention, so the graph cannot loop forever. If it abstains, the worker falls back to single-pass retrieval.

trace.name: Scoped retrieval
trace.note: The search function accepts only a query. Tenant and client IDs come from server code and select the Pinecone namespace, so message text cannot widen the search.

trace.name: Confidence check
trace.note: Below the client's threshold, the system sends a configured fallback, or sends nothing and logs the event. The page token is decrypted only just before sending.

decisions: Kept tenant and client identity out of the model's input instead of relying on prompt wording.
Put tenant filtering in one database wrapper, because the service role key bypasses row-level security.
Stored Meta tokens with AES-256-GCM, and added a source scan that fails on known leak patterns.
Logged the main outcomes separately: skipped, low confidence, failed and sent.
tested: Tenant isolation: 22 of 22, against a mock Supabase client, not a real database.
Token leak: 19 of 19. This scans source text and does not run the system.
Whole suite on 2026-11-07: 56 passed, 9 failed, 1 suite did not load.
The failures are upstream tests. Seven cover the parser and an older feature-flag API, two need an API key, and one suite imports a route that no longer exists.
limits: The worker and agent graph have no automated tests, and no live run is verified.
If a send succeeds and logging then hits a temporary error, a retry could send the reply again.
Once autopilot is on, replies go out with no human review, and the current prompt tells the model not to reveal automation. Both need a decision before any real customer use.
A newer database schema is documented as verified, but the application has not been moved to it.
The README still carries upstream DocsFlow text.

projects.name: EduSmartAI
projects.problem: An academic platform needed to warn about struggling students early, but its old 0.979 score relied on data only known after a course ended.
built: On a branch of a graduation project by @bahaaed07706: early-risk models for day 14, 28 and 42, using only data visible by that day.
Student-grouped validation, a temporal holdout and confidence intervals.
Shared feature code for training and serving, rule-based explanations and intervention tracking.
Token revocation, audit logging, rate limiting, and a PostgreSQL path.
works: Models retrained from the branch reproduce its reported results.
ROC-AUC rises from 0.566 at day 14, close to chance, to 0.729 at day 42.
Backend security, intervention and serving behavior pass their tests.
projects.architecture: FastAPI and SQLAlchemy backend, scikit-learn pipelines per cut-off, and a React frontend with Arabic and English.
projects.stack: Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, React

evidence.text: Retrained on 2026-11-07: ROC-AUC 0.566, 0.677 and 0.729, matching the report.
Backend tests: 220 passed, 3 skipped, at commit 73583aa.
Frontend tests and the live PostgreSQL integration were not run.

projects.status: Branch not merged. PR #7 was closed with no review.
projects.role: EduSmartAI is a graduation project by @bahaaed07706, who built and owns it. He had already documented that the old 0.979 was inflated by leakage, and he wrote the retriever. My branch builds the replacement models and the backend hardening around them. Its commits credit an AI coding agent as co-author.

trace.name: Course activity
trace.note: Attendance, submissions and engagement records for each student and course.

trace.name: Temporal cut-off
trace.note: At day 14, 28 or 42, only events visible by that day are used, which avoids the leakage in the old evaluation.

trace.name: Group-aware validation
trace.note: StratifiedGroupKFold keeps each student on one side of every split, with a temporal holdout and bootstrap confidence intervals.

trace.name: Early-risk model
trace.note: A scikit-learn pipeline per cut-off, trained so that scaling and encoding happen inside each fold.

trace.name: Train-serve parity
trace.note: Training and serving share one feature module, and tests check that they produce the same features.

trace.name: Explanation
trace.note: Deterministic, rule-based explanations of which signals drove a prediction, with no model-generated text.

trace.name: Intervention
trace.note: Staff can record and track actions taken for a flagged student.

decisions: Reported that the day-14 model is close to chance, and called it insufficient for operational use, instead of tuning until it looked better.
Built replacement models after the project owner documented the leakage in the old 0.979.
Added server-side token revocation, audit logging and rate limiting to the backend.
Added a bilingual held-out RAG evaluation, Arabic right-to-left support and accessibility work.
tested: ROC-AUC by cut-off: day 14, 0.5657. Day 28, 0.6769. Day 42, 0.7288.
Accuracy by cut-off: day 14, 0.5536. Day 28, 0.6444. Day 42, 0.6844.
Backend suite: 220 passed, 3 skipped, at commit 73583aa.
limits: The legacy 0.979 could not be reproduced, because a source file is not in the repository.
The branch is not part of the project's main branch.
The retriever is by the project owner, and it is lexical, not semantic.
Live LLM answer quality was not evaluated. Frontend tests and the live PostgreSQL integration were not run.

projects.name: Shortform Pro
projects.problem: An unattended video pipeline can look healthy while publishing the wrong thing. Over 90 days, version 1 logged 356 uploads with only 12 distinct titles.
built: Version 1: my own Python and FFmpeg pipeline, publishing daily to YouTube through GitHub Actions.
Version 2, built in November 2026 with an AI coding agent at my direction: a rebuild after auditing version 1.
A content state machine, measured quality checks, approval tied to the exact file, and a publish gate.
works: A real upload is blocked unless approval, live mode, a confirmation phrase and the channel ID all match.
An uncertain upload moves to a state that a person must resolve, so a retry cannot post a duplicate.
Rendered Arabic and English samples pass measured checks for format, silence and loudness.
projects.architecture: Python pipeline, FFmpeg rendering, durable JSON state with an event log, and the YouTube Data API behind a gate.
projects.stack: Python, FFmpeg, Edge TTS, libass, GitHub Actions, YouTube Data API

evidence.text: 200 tests passed on 2026-11-07, all with fake publishers.
4 rendered samples measured between -16.0 and -16.3 LUFS. No person has listened to them yet.
Upload history counted from the state file: 356 uploads, 12 titles, one published 80 times.
Version 2 has never uploaded a video.

projects.status: Version 1 is paused. Version 2 is local, and has never uploaded.

media.alt: Eight frames from a rendered Arabic explainer video about why the sky is blue, showing animated diagrams and captions.
media.caption: Frames from a real rendered sample. It has not been published.

projects.role: I wrote version 1. The audit and version 2 were done in November 2026 with an AI coding agent, Claude Code, working at my direction. Those commits credit it as co-author.
projects.trace_title: One video, from script to platform

trace.name: Script catalog
trace.note: Scripts come from a versioned catalog, and each factual claim lists a source. The pipeline makes no LLM call at run time. Duplicates are detected by file hash, title and narration.

trace.name: Narration and captions
trace.note: Per-sentence speech synthesis with word timings, and captions with correct Arabic shaping and right-to-left order.

trace.name: Render
trace.note: Motion graphics in code, a ducked music bed and two-pass loudness normalization, rendered with FFmpeg.

trace.name: Measured checks
trace.note: Streams, delivery settings, black frames, silence, loudness, peaks and caption timing are measured from the file. A failed check stops the item.

trace.name: Human approval
trace.note: Approval is tied to the exact file hash. If the file changes, the approval no longer applies.

trace.name: Publish gate
trace.note: A real upload needs live mode, a written confirmation phrase and the expected channel ID. The default is a dry run.

trace.name: Idempotent slot
trace.note: Each slot can publish once. If an upload fails after the platform may have received it, the item moves to a reconciliation state for a person to check, so a retry cannot post a duplicate.

decisions: Paused version 1 once the audit showed that green CI runs were hiding repeated uploads.
Moved state out of a database that vanished after each CI run, into durable state with atomic writes.
Made routing fail on an unknown schedule instead of guessing, after a cron typo sent English slots to Arabic.
Measured what can be measured, and left creative judgment to a person.
tested: 200 automated tests passed on 2026-11-07, all with fake publishers.
4 rendered samples, Arabic and English, passed measured checks.
Upload history counted from the state file: 356 uploads, 12 distinct titles.
limits: No person has listened to the samples yet, so their quality is unjudged.
Version 2 has never uploaded, so its live publishing path is unverified and its effect on viewers is unknown.
Facebook, Instagram and TikTok publishing does not work.
Version 2 is not pushed, so the public repository still shows version 1.

about: I am an AI Engineer in Amman with a B.Sc. in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence from Philadelphia University. The part of AI work I care about most starts after the first demo: can it be measured, can it be stopped, and what happens when something fails?

That is why my projects look the way they do. They track evidence, separate tenants and wait for approval. Most of them build on existing software instead of starting from nothing, and each one says so. I also use AI coding agents in my work, and the project pages say where that is known.

approach.title: Measure before claiming
approach.text: Evaluation comes with the system, and a missing measurement stays missing.

approach.title: Keep authority out of the model
approach.text: Scope and permissions live in server code, where a prompt cannot change them.

approach.title: Give automation a stopping point
approach.text: Risky steps wait for a check or a person, and retries cannot repeat them.

approach.title: Report what the data supports
approach.text: When a strong number comes from a flawed test, I replace it and explain why.

experience.lead: This work is private, so I describe it at a high level.
points: Designed and tested LLM, RAG and AI-agent workflows using Python, n8n, REST APIs and webhooks, with validation, escalation logic and human-in-the-loop controls.
Built and evaluated AWS Bedrock RAG experiments with S3-backed knowledge sources and citation-grounded test cases.
Mapped workflows with internal teams, and analyzed SOC alert investigation and reporting as an AI-assisted analyst use case.
Applied Apache Spark and PySpark to data and machine-learning workflows, contributed to LLM and RAG application work, and built Power BI dashboards.
